scope: Original synthetic development pilot; no real research results

cases.author_priority: Explain the benefit and tradeoff of observation-age-aware robot scheduling, preserving both timing and task outcomes.
facts: A visual grasping controller receives asynchronous camera frames. In its serial implementation, queued older observations can be used while a new frame waits for action generation.
The proposed scheduler chooses the latest completed frame at each action-generation start and discards older queued frames. It uses the same policy weights as the serial implementation.
Evaluation uses the same GPU, four moving-object grasping tasks, 80 physical robot executions per task and per method, and the same pretraining and task-demonstration data.

Mean observation-to-command time is 96 ms with serial scheduling, 62 ms with a faster action decoder alone, and 41 ms with observation-age-aware scheduling. These times include waiting, preprocessing and action generation, but not command-to-motion time.
Task-average success is 61% for serial scheduling, 62% for the faster decoder and 74% for observation-age-aware scheduling. No uncertainty estimates are supplied.
The scheduler drops 18% of arriving frames on this workload. The evaluation does not isolate observation freshness from all other scheduling changes.

cases.author_priority: Communicate a diagnosis of aggregate-score sensitivity to task weighting, rather than present a new better-performing policy.
facts: Two warehouse-navigation policies are evaluated on fixed routes: short routes and long routes. Their outputs do not change when score aggregation weights change.
Policy U succeeds on 90% of short routes and 40% of long routes; policy V succeeds on 75% of short routes and 70% of long routes.
A dashboard weights short and long routes 9:1, yielding 85% aggregate success for U and 74.5% for V. Equal task-family weighting yields 65% for U and 72.5% for V.
The study derives the two weighted means and replays the same recorded outputs under both aggregation rules. There is no retraining or new policy.
The authors provide a report showing both task-family scores beside each aggregate score. The report is applied to the existing fixed-route evaluation; it has no measured effect on deployed safety.
Route-family execution counts and uncertainty are not supplied. No claim of statistical significance is licensed.

cases.author_priority: Explain what a wrist-camera viewpoint benchmark can test and the baseline finding it exposes; dataset size is supporting detail.
facts: A grasping benchmark records the same objects and manipulation tasks using six wrist-camera mounting positions. Existing evaluation in this project kept mounting position fixed.

The released benchmark has 2400 demonstration episodes. Episode-disjoint training and validation data use three mount positions; testing uses three different mounts. Objects and task instructions remain shared across the split.
The protocol measures transfer across camera mounting positions, not unseen objects, unseen tasks, new robots or zero-shot learning without training.

A baseline trained on the training mounts reaches 84% success on validation mounts from that training group and 57% on held-out mounts. Fine-tuning with 30 demonstrations from the held-out mounts raises success there to 72%.
The baseline architecture is not a new contribution. The adaptation result uses additional target-mount data; model selection uses the original validation split.
The benchmark and split definitions are released. Evaluation-trial counts, uncertainty, and a universal robustness guarantee are not supplied.
